title: I Will Find Her
mood: A map full of red crosses, a telescope at night, a gate she will not pass back through, and a window left lit.

hero.alt: In front of the white Academy building, pink-haired Guinevere stands alone and quiet, holding a small gold star up against her chest.
hero.credit: Official Guinevere and Vexana interactive drama

segs.t: The map covered Guinevere’s whole bed. She had drawn a grid over Terrinia in red ink, one square for every sector she was cleared to fly.
The star at her collar had been lit every hour since the corridor. It could not tell her where.
It could beep, though. On the roof it had beeped when Vexana came within half a roof of her.
Half a roof, then,
she thought.
Over every street in the city.
She taped her split knuckles and took the first square.
She flew it low over the roofs, her two drones at her shoulders. At the end of the row she hung in the air over a chimney and tapped the star.
“Come on,” she told it. “Beep.”
It glowed and said nothing.
When her drones began to skim the chimneys, she flew home and put a red cross through every square she had flown. The next night she took the next row.
The star never beeped.
By the time every square had one cross through it, the tape on her knuckles had gone gray. Late one night she went to the Science Division.
Light came from under Chang’e’s door. Guinevere knocked and went in.
Notes on the void glowed on every screen. Chang’e was asleep at her console, her cheek on her arm. Mr. Bunny hung at her shoulder.
She coughed in her sleep. A frown came up on Mr. Bunny’s screen.
Lesley came in past her with a cup of water and one small pill, and set them by Chang’e’s elbow.
Chang’e woke and looked at the pill.
“Eleven hours of sleep in six days,” said Lesley. “Drink.”
“I’m fine. It’s a cold. Colds are optional.”
Lesley did not argue. She leaned on the door frame beside Guinevere and folded her arms.
Chang’e glared at her. Lesley waited.
“I hate scary Big Sis!” said Chang’e.
Then she swallowed the pill and drank the water in one go.
Lesley took the empty cup and left without a word.
Chang’e saw Guinevere in the doorway. Her glance went to the screens.
“I told your class I’d never send a student anywhere I couldn’t bring them back from,” she said. “Nobody sent her.”
“Then help me bring her back,” said Guinevere. “Something that can find the far side of a door.”
“I can’t even find the door.” Chang’e waved a hand at the glowing screens. “That’s all of it, and it’s nothing.”
She pointed at Guinevere’s collar.
“That’s the only thing still answering her. Ruby comes in the morning for Angela’s check. Ask her. She does in four seconds what takes me a week.”
In the morning Guinevere came back with the star unpinned and shut in her fist. It was still lit.

The lab door stood open. Angela sat on the lab bench with her hands flat on its edge, her little doll clipped at her hip. Ruby sat on a stool beside her. Chang’e held a tablet half her size. On its list, beside one line, she had written a word by hand. WEEKLY.
Guinevere stopped in the doorway.
Ruby looked up. Her eyes went to Guinevere and the light between her fingers, then back to Angela.
She laid her gloved hand on the bench. Green lines ran up the screen. A red square came up, and a triangle marked DANGER.
“If Oro ever takes you again,” said Ruby, “this lets me stop you. If I delete it, nothing does.”
She said it flat. Then she turned to Angela. “You’re the one who controls yourself. What to do is yours to decide.”
Ruby did not say which answer she wanted.
Angela looked at the red square for a long time. Then she nodded.
The lock opened under Ruby’s hand. Forty lines scrolled down the screen and blinked out one by one, until nothing was left under Angela’s walking routines but walking.
“Now you’re free. Forever,” said Ruby.
Chang’e drew a line through the last entry on her list. “Neat code,” she said. “Shame to delete it.”
“Not really,” said Ruby.
Mr. Bunny drifted down from Chang’e’s shoulder. He stopped in front of the doll at Angela’s hip, close enough to touch its face.
Chang’e’s voice went soft. “Look! Mr. Bunny, it’s a new friend for you.”
Ruby leaned on the bench. “My turn. Angela, what do you want the most?”
Angela looked straight at Ruby. She did not stop to think.
“I want to protect everyone!” said Angela.
Ruby laughed once. Angela smiled back at her, a hand’s width away.
In the doorway, Guinevere’s hand closed tight around the star.
“You’ve been standing there a while,” said Ruby.
Guinevere opened her hand. “Can you make this a tracker? It beeps when she’s close. I need it to tell me where.”
Angela took the star in both cupped hands, as if it might spill. Ruby laid her fingertips beside it, and green lines ran into the gold.
Guinevere stood over them with her arms folded. Her left bow hung crooked.
“The glow is the same at every reading,” said Ruby. “It doesn’t fade with distance. It doesn’t point.”
“Then make it point.”
“It has no direction, Guinevere. It only says yes.”
Angela looked down at the light in her hands. “Then yes is something.”
Selena passed the bench with a lollipop in her cheek, Silverbolt clicking at her heel. She glanced at the gold star in Angela’s hands.
“Lost things turn up,” she said, to nobody.
She was out the door before anyone answered.
Guinevere took her star back and pinned it at her collar.
That night, after her row, she waited in her room until the hour Vexana used to call had come and gone. Then she climbed the stairs to the top of the Academy’s tower.
The observation lab was a glass room under the beam. Ruby and Angela kept the tower’s sensor array running up there at night. A long telescope stood at the glass, pointed at nothing.
“The lab is closed at night, Guinevere,” said Ruby, in her perfect voice.
“It is,” said Angela, from a panel. “You should go.”
“Then I’m not here.” Guinevere lit the lamp beside the telescope and put her eye to the lens.
Angela looked at her a while. “What are you looking for?”
“A door,” said Guinevere. “Anything that isn’t a star.”
She moved the telescope across the sky one small piece at a time, until dawn. In the night log beside Ruby’s console she wrote one word.
Nothing.
The next night they both asked her to leave. On the third night nobody asked. Angela pushed a stool over to the telescope with her foot.

blocks.caption: The tower’s glass lab, two night keepers, and one telescope.

media.alt: In a glass-walled lab high above a cloudy city, Ruby holds a long telescope, Guinevere stands between the two with a hand on the gold star at her chest, and Angela watches with a finger at her lips.
media.credit: Official Guinevere and Vexana interactive drama

segs.t: The log filled up with
Nothing.
At lunch Layla set her tray down across the long table.
“Portals don’t give people back,” she said.
“She’s alive,” said Guinevere.
She unpinned the star and held it out on her fingertips. It glowed gold over her untouched tray.
“It’s a circuit, Guinevere,” said Layla, not unkindly. “Circuits glitch.”
“Leave her be, Layla,” said Fanny.
Angela put down her spoon. “No. I came back once. People come back.”
Guinevere turned the star so its seams caught the light. “I soldered every seam myself.”
“The Aspirant spirit never lies,” she said.
Nobody argued. She pinned the star back on and took her tray away.
Behind her, at another table, someone said, “The claw was meant for Baroque. Vexana took it.”
Her step did not change. She had written it down herself, on the corridor floor.
“Daddy will buy her a new partner,” said someone else.
Guinevere turned around. “The great lady Guinevere, if you please.”
She walked on with her chin high.
One morning a clerk from the records office stood under the board outside the Combat office, a form in his hand. The sheet with VEXANA: MISSING still hung above him. Lesley read the form standing up.
Guinevere stopped behind them. Her knuckles had scabbed over by then.
“No trace since the corridor,” said the clerk. “After this long, the form says Killed in action.”
Lesley folded her arms. “No body, no finding. Her file says Missing. It stays Missing.”
The clerk took his form back and went.
Guinevere stepped in front of her. “Then give me a squad. I’ll lead it.”
“Give me a lead and I’ll give you a squad.”
“The star is lit.”
“That’s a light,” said Lesley. “Not a lead.”
Her eye stayed on Guinevere a moment longer. Then she went into her office and shut the door.
By then every square on the map had three red crosses through it. All that was left lay past the outer ward’s fence, where the dome came down to the dead ground.
She flew there one night at the end of a long row. By the time she reached it her power was spent. She landed and climbed.
The fence was wire, twice her height. One lamp burned over its gate. She was halfway up when a hand caught her collar and pulled her back down.
A Shield sergeant, gray at the temples, a rifle on his back. He looked at her pink hair and her two red bows, and she watched him work out who she was.
“No pass, no entry, miss.”
“I will find her, no matter what,” said Guinevere.
“Then do it with a pass.”
He walked her back under the lamp and wrote her name in his book.
Two mornings later the counseling section sent for her.
The room had soft chairs and a window full of plants. An older woman poured tea into two cups and held one out.
“Sit down, Guinevere. Tell me about her.”
Guinevere sat down. “She’s alive.”
Then she stood up and left. The tea stayed full on the table.
The next morning a guard called her to the gate.
Hester was waiting outside the bars in her gray coat. Behind her the long car stood with its back door open.
“Miss Guinevere. Your father sends word.”
He sent word,
thought Guinevere.

She had written to him every week since she came to the Academy. The only answer had come through Hester: a board meeting. At the trial and at the ceremony, the House’s seat had stayed empty. Both times Hester had sat two rows behind it.
Her hand found one of the bars.

Hester did not soften it. “A Shield sergeant reported you at a closed fence, at night. A student was taken inside the Academy’s own walls. You are to come home. If you do not, your place in the House is gone.”
Guinevere waited for more. A word about her. Any word.
“Is that all he said?”
“That is all.”
The bar was cold under her palm. Past Hester she could see the open car, and the seat she had ridden in to this gate on the morning of the assessment. She could be in that seat in a minute.
At her collar, the star was warm.
“I won’t stop. I still have something to protect,” said Guinevere.
She let go of the bar.
“Then tell him he’ll see,” she said. “Once I bring her back.”
Hester inclined her head a single degree. Then she spoke very low.
“He reads the Academy’s lists every morning, miss.”
She did not say which list. The rankings, or the one with the dead.

Guinevere opened her mouth to ask. Hester was looking at her left bow, hanging crooked. She had tied those bows first, the morning Guinevere’s hair was long enough. Her hand came up to the bars and stopped there.
Her eyes went down to Guinevere’s hands, to the new pink skin across her knuckles.
“Hands home after every punch, miss.”
Guinevere’s throat had shut. She nodded once.
Then she turned and walked back across the courtyard.
On the morning of the assessment the gate had clanged shut behind her, and she had turned to find Hester through the bars. Today she did not turn. If she turned, she would go.
She counted her steps under her breath instead. Hester had once counted the cellar stairs that way, so a child in the dark would not cry.
Behind her no car door shut, and no engine started. Hester stayed where she was.
Under the billboard Guinevere stopped. Two girls back to back, one with a pink ponytail, one with long black hair. THEIR UNDEFEATED RECORD HAS MADE THEM LEGENDS EVEN AMONG THE ASPIRANTS!
She used to salute it. Now she touched her collar.
Lit. She went in.
That night she did not climb the tower.
At the hour Vexana used to call, she sat on the sill of her own window with the phone in her lap. It did not ring. She held it anyway.
He reads the lists,
she thought.
Every morning. And I never once knew he was looking.
So you might be looking too, Vexana, wherever you are. Then look here.
She set her lamp on the sill beside her and left it burning.
Past the city’s lights the dome curved down to its edge. Past the edge lay the dark, and nothing in it she could see.
She laid two fingers on the star at her collar.
“O dark night, do you, too, long for starlight?” she asked the dark.
It gave no answer. Below her one square of light lay on the grass, her own. Along the rest of the wing the grass was dark.
She stayed in the window with the lamp at her side. Its warmth lay along her cheek.
Toward morning the sky past the dome went gray. Her window was still lit, and so was the small gold star at her collar.
